title: What I like
topic: aimer, adorer, détester, préférer + definite article or infinitive; moi aussi / moi non plus
why: Now that you can describe people, you learn to talk about tastes: what you love, like, prefer or can't stand, and how to react to someone else's tastes. The key point is the definite article after aimer, where English uses no article at all.

{"lessons": ["

J'aime le chocolat: the article English leaves out

To talk about tastes, you have a whole scale of regular -er verbs, from love to hate. Préférer has the stem change you know: je préfère, nous préférons.

FrenchEnglish
J'adore…I love…
J'aime beaucoup…I really like…
J'aime bien…I like…, I quite like…
Je n'aime pas beaucoup…I don't really like…
Je n'aime pas…I don't like…
Je déteste…I hate…
Je préfère…I prefer…

Here is the key point. English says “I like chocolate”, “I love movies”, “I hate rain”, with no article. French always needs the definite article after these verbs, because you're talking about the thing in general: J'aime le chocolat, J'adore les films, Je déteste la pluie, Je préfère l'été. Never j'aime chocolat, and never du: du chocolat means some chocolate, a quantity.

A taste (in general)A quantity (some)
J'aime le fromage.Je prends du fromage.
J'adore la confiture.Je voudrais de la confiture.
Je préfère l'eau.Je bois de l'eau.

The negative keeps the article

You learned that du / de la / des become de after ne… pas. That rule does not apply to le / la / les: Je n'aime pas le café, Il ne déteste pas les chats. Saying je n'aime pas de café is one of the most frequent mistakes.

With things you can count, use the plural: J'adore les croissants, Je n'aime pas les chiens. With a singular noun, French means the thing as a substance or an idea: le fromage, la musique, le sport.

", "

Aimer + infinitive, and aimer with people

To say you like doing something, put the second verb in the infinitive, as after vouloir or pouvoir. English often uses an -ing form here (“I love traveling”); French never does.

J'aime lire le soir.I like reading in the evening.
Ma sœur adore voyager, mais elle déteste attendre à l'aéroport.My sister loves traveling, but she hates waiting at the airport.
Je n'aime pas cuisiner. Je préfère faire la vaisselle !I don't like cooking. I prefer doing the dishes!

Je t'aime or je t'aime bien?

With things, bien makes aimer a little softer: J'aime bien le jazz (I quite like jazz). With people, the difference is huge. Je t'aime means “I love you” (a partner, your children, your parents). Je t'aime bien means “I like you” (a friend, a colleague). Adding bien, which normally means “well”, makes it weaker, not stronger: a classic misunderstanding for English speakers!

Take t' in je t'aime as a fixed form for now: pronouns like this one are the topic of the next lesson. For a person in general, simply say J'aime bien Thomas, Il est sympa.

Ça me plaît

You'll also hear Ça me plaît (I like it; literally “it pleases me”) and the question Ça te plaît ? (Do you like it?). Learn them as fixed expressions: Lyon ? Ça me plaît beaucoup !

Never say j'aime bien to your partner if you mean love: it sounds like friendship. And don't say je t'aime to a new colleague!

", "

Me too, me neither: hobbies

Reacting to what someone likes is easy in French, as long as you watch whether the first sentence is positive or negative.

They say…You agreeYou disagree
J'aime le jazz.Moi aussi. (me too)Pas moi. (not me)
Je n'aime pas le jazz.Moi non plus. (me neither)Moi si. (I do)

The English trap: after a negative sentence, “me neither” is moi non plus, never moi aussi. And si is the yes that contradicts a negative, as you saw with questions: — Je n'aime pas le fromage. — Moi si ! J'adore ça.

Jouer à, jouer de, faire de

English “play” covers sports, games and instruments. French splits them:

PatternUsed forExamples
jouer à (au, à la, aux)sports and gamesjouer au foot, au tennis, aux cartes
jouer de (du, de la, des)musical instrumentsjouer du piano, de la guitare, du violon
faire de (du, de la, de l')activities, many sportsfaire du vélo, du yoga, de la natation, de la randonnée
Mon frère joue au foot le samedi et ma sœur joue de la guitare.My brother plays soccer on Saturdays and my sister plays the guitar.
— Tu fais du sport ? — Oui, je fais de la natation et du vélo.— Do you do any sport? — Yes, I swim and I cycle.

Remember the contractions: à + le = au, de + le = du. So jouer au tennis but jouer du piano.
